title: Christians (Acts 11:19–26)
hook: in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tabitha of Joppa, and the coats she made for the widows. Your line was she was full of good works.

For the first years after Jesus, his followers had no one name. In Acts they're the disciples, the brethren, the saints, the believers, and people of the Way. Then, in a big, noisy, mixed city in Syria, somebody gave them a name. The text doesn't say who. And the name stuck. It started in a single city, at a single moment, and Luke wrote the moment down.
screen: `DISCIPLES, BRETHREN, THE WAY.` → `NO ONE NAME YET.` → `THEN, ONE CITY.`

segments.voice: The city is Antioch, a great city of Roman Syria. After Stephen's death, believers scattered and spoke the word only to fellow Jews. But some men from Cyprus and Cyrene came to Antioch and spoke to Greeks as well, and a great number believed. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, the son of encouragement. He sees what's happening, and the text says he was glad. Then he does something wise: he goes to Tarsus to find Saul, the new convert from Damascus, and brings him back. The two of them teach in Antioch for a whole year. Then the line, in the Douay-Rheims: "at Antioch the disciples were first named Christians." In Greek, Christianoi. The ending is a Latin-style one, used for a party or a household: Caesar's people, Herod's people. So the name likely meant Christ's people, the Messiah's crowd. Some readers think outsiders coined it, maybe half as a joke. The word turns up again from King Agrippa's lips later in Acts, and in First Peter, where believers are told not to be ashamed if they suffer as one. So a name perhaps given by neighbors became a name people were willing to die for. Antioch has another place in Catholic memory. Tradition says Peter led the church there before Rome. And a later bishop of Antioch, Ignatius, wrote a letter that calls the Church catholic, meaning universal.
screen: `ANTIOCH: JEWS AND GREEKS TOGETHER.` · `BARNABAS FETCHES SAUL.` · `CHRISTIANOI: CHRIST'S PEOPLE.` · `A NICKNAME BECOMES A NAME.` · then, large: `FIRST CALLED CHRISTIANS.`

segments.voice: Sit for a moment with a name you carry, by faith or family or job. If you are a Christian, notice that the word may first have come from neighbors who watched how believers lived; if the name isn't yours, think of one you do carry, a family name, a team, a title, and what it asks of you. No grading, just noticing, and if you pray, ask to live up to your name.
Christian. Christ's people, the Messiah's people, a name first heard in Antioch and perhaps given by outsiders. Today's word.
Your line: first called christians. Tomorrow, a knock at a gate in the night. That's day five hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics receive their Christian name at baptism, often a saint's name, and the Church keeps the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter on February 22, which once had a separate celebration for Peter's chair at Antioch.

original.note: Greek: Christian, one of Christ's people. Christos means anointed.

trapdoor: what you thought: the name Christians gave themselves.
what it means: in Antioch, where Jews and Greeks believed together, the disciples were first called by a name probably given by others.

what a scholar hears: the -ianos ending is a Latin-style party label, like Herodians. the word turns up again in Acts 26 and 1 Peter 4, and Ignatius of Antioch's letter to the Smyrnaeans is often cited as an early use of 'catholic church'.
recall: martys: one who tells what they saw

chat.says: Where did the name Christian come from? Did Jesus give it to his followers?
options: Acts says the disciples were first called that in Antioch, maybe by outsiders.
Jesus gave it to the twelve at the Last Supper as their new name.
The apostles chose it in Jerusalem so believers would stand apart.
chat.meaning: Acts says the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. The name meant Christ's people, and it may have come from outsiders.

Antioch.meaning: a great city of Roman Syria

Agrippa.meaning: a king who uses the word later in Acts

Ignatius.meaning: a later bishop of Antioch who called the Church catholic

notes: Acts 11:26 paraphrased: the Douay-Rheims wording ('first named Christians'?) was not certain enough to quote.
'More than two billion people' is a common estimate of Christians worldwide; confirm.
The -ianus/-ianos ending and outsiders coining the name: widely held scholarly view, not certain; confirm hedging.
Tradition of Peter at Antioch; the separate feast of the Chair of Peter at Antioch (formerly February 22 with Rome on January 18) merged in 1960; confirm the howItsDone wording.
Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 8, earliest surviving use of 'catholic church': standard claim; confirm.
